note: Synthetic examples. No real client data.

problem_statement.summary: A 60-store specialty coffee chain has seen same-store sales fall 7% year over year.
problem_statement.key_question: Why are same-store sales declining and how can the chain return to growth within a year?

issue_tree.question: Why are same-store sales declining and how can the chain return to growth?

hypotheses.statement: Morning traffic has shifted to new drive-through competitors.
hypotheses.rationale: Sales = traffic x ticket; competitor openings reported

hypotheses.statement: Fewer customers add food items, lowering average ticket.
hypotheses.rationale: Food attach rate is a common ticket driver

workstreams.name: Traffic
analytical_questions: Do declines correlate with competitor openings?

workstreams.name: Ticket
analytical_questions: How has food attach rate changed?

frameworks.name: Customer segmentation
frameworks.rationale: Commuter and leisure customers behave differently

mece_check.notes: Same-store sales decomposes exactly into traffic and ticket.

problem_statement.summary: An industrial pump manufacturer earns 90% of revenue from new equipment and wants to build an aftermarket services business.
problem_statement.key_question: Should the company build an aftermarket services business, and if so, how should it enter?

issue_tree.question: Should the company build an aftermarket services business, and how?

children.question: How large and profitable is the addressable installed base?
Can the company win against independent service providers?
What entry model maximizes value (build, partner, acquire)?

hypotheses.statement: The installed base supports a services market with margins above new-equipment margins.
OEM parts knowledge gives a defensible advantage over independents.
A partner-led entry reaches scale faster than an organic build.

workstreams.name: Market attractiveness
workstreams.objective: Size and profitability of the aftermarket
analytical_questions: What is the installed base by segment?

workstreams.name: Right to win
analytical_questions: What do customers value in service providers?

frameworks.name: SWOT
frameworks.rationale: Summarize capability fit per entry model

mece_check.notes: Where to play (attractiveness), how to win, and how to enter are distinct and complete.

problem_statement.summary: A regional airline's on-time performance fell from 82% to 68%; delays cascade through a hub-and-spoke network. Data quality on delay codes is poor.
problem_statement.key_question: What is driving the on-time performance decline and which interventions restore performance above 80%?

issue_tree.question: What drives the on-time decline and which interventions restore it?

children.question: Is the schedule less able to absorb delays (propagation)?

hypotheses.statement: Aircraft maintenance delays have risen as the fleet ages.
Ground-handling turnarounds at the hub exceed scheduled times.
Schedule buffers were cut, so delays propagate further.

workstreams.name: Delay data reconstruction
workstreams.objective: Rebuild reliable delay attribution because delay codes are unreliable
analytical_questions: Can timestamps replace delay codes for attribution?

workstreams.name: Maintenance
analytical_questions: How have mechanical delays changed by aircraft age?

workstreams.name: Schedule resilience
workstreams.objective: Measure delay propagation and buffer adequacy

frameworks.name: Value chain analysis
frameworks.rationale: Trace delay sources across the operation

mece_check.notes: Root delays and propagation interact; WS0 is a data prerequisite rather than a branch. Treat overlap explicitly when attributing impact.
